newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's Van Miert warns of liberalisation delays.
newsitem.headline: EU's Van Miert warns of liberalisation delays.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert warned on Thursday of slower progress in opening up EU markets to competition, saying signs for liberalisation were not good.
"The current weather conditions for liberalisation are not good," Van Miert told a conference on the future of liberalisation.
The effects of "a more sunny period" for deregulation just before the launch of the European Union's single market in 1993 broke down barriers for trade were being felt now, he said.
The airline sector was being opened up to competition as a result but further progress could take longer than expected.
He did not elaborate on the reasons for this, but Europe's high unemployment rate of 11 percent is one likely factor as member member states fear more competition could mean more job losses.

Powerful unions argue that liberalisation risks destroying jobs but industry and the Commission insist it is needed to boost the competitive power of the EU, which is lagging behind the United States and Japan, partly because of costly services.

Britain, Germany and the Nordic countries tend to favour fast and far-reaching liberalisation while France and southern EU member states are more reluctant, fearing it could endanger the supply of essential services at an affordable price.

Progress has been particularly slow in politically sensitive areas such as postal markets. Van Miert said time would be needed to open up the post to competition, "but putting things off is no solution".

He said the EU executive had no plans to use its wide powers under Article 90 of the Treaty of Rome to force governments to open up the sector but "there should be no misunderstanding that (EU) competition rules remain and should be applicable to the postal sector".
EU member states are divided over how quickly to allow private operators to compete with state post offices to deliver direct mail and incoming cross-border mail.

Van Miert expressed disappointment with the compromise deal on a gradual and partial liberalisation of electricity markets reached by EU energy ministers after years of wrangling, saying it was "not going to meet the challenges of modern times".

The agreement reached at a special ministerial session last June was a hard-fought compromise between countries such as Germany and Britain, which wanted extensive liberalisation, and France, which is wary of any dramatic moves.

Under the compromise -- which still has to be approved by the European Parliament -- nearly a quarter of the EU's overall market for electricity will be open to competition from January 1999. This will rise to nearly a third by 2003.
Van Miert said he hoped market forces would ensure further liberalisation although actions in Belgium and Italy did not give grounds for excessive optimism.

He referred to the plan by Belgian electricity producer Electrabel to lock local authorities into exclusive long-term supply contracts and steps in Italy to oblige independent producers to sell to state-owned ENEL only.
"While on the one hand things seem to develop beyond the (EU directive on electricity liberalisation), at the same time practices are developed in the opposite way," he said.
Following the deal on electricity, EU energy officials hope it will be easier to agree to open up natural gas markets, even though member states remain far apart on key issues.
